newsitem.title: PERU: World pressure grows on defiant Peru guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: World pressure grows on defiant Peru guerrillas.

text.p: International pressure grew on Friday on the defiant Peruvian Marxist guerrillas holding 103 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence for the 10th day.

In the toughest of a long stream of appeals to the rebels from around the world, the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations weighed in to condemn the hostage-takers as "terrorists" and promised to help the Peruvian government with "all the appropriate means that it could request."

Stressing the principle of no concessions to armed rebels, the G7 communique coincided with reports a U.S. spyplane had made high-altitude night flights over the residence and crack anti-terrorist units of the Peruvian police were training around a model of the building.

The comunique was issued by France, which holds the organisation's rotating presidency. It said the group -- along with Russia -- "reaffirmed the general principle under which no concession must be made in the face of a terrorist action" and that G7 countries "express their solidarity with the Peruvian government and support its efforts to resolve the crisis peacefully, with the main objective of sparing human lives."
Shortly after the statement was issued, Peruvian ministers arrived at the government palace in downtown Lima for an emergency cabinet meeting with President Alberto Fujimori.

Earlier on Friday, Japan, whose nationals account for the largest number of hostages after Peru, called for unity in resolving the crisis. "It is clear that the international community should not condone terrorism," Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told a news conference. "It is also necessary ... to act as one to help resolve this crisis by setting free all the hostages peacefully, and at an early date."
In Bonn, German Foreign Ministry spokesman Martin Erdmann told Reuters G7 ambassadors had met in Lima to discuss their next step. "Their main objective is to avoid violence," Erdmann said.

The hardening position of the international community followed Christmas appeals from around the world, including Pope John Paul II and U.S. President Bill Clinton, for the rebels to change their position. But the roughly 20 guerrillas holed up inside the booby-trapped residence showed no signs on Friday of softening their conditions for releasing hostages.

They have released around 400 captives since they stormed the building on Dec. 17, keeping those they consider most useful as bargaining chips, including two Peruvian ministers, Japanese businessmen, some foreign diplomats and the brother of Fujimori.
They are demanding the release of around 400 jailed comrades in Peru, followed by safe passage -- with some hostages as guarantors -- to an Amazon jungle stronghold.

Fujimori, who spoke in public just once since the rebels stormed a party at the ambassador's residence, refused to negotiate with them directly and has flatly rejected their demand for prisoner releases. He also ignored pleas by hostages to reconnect the building's electricity and water.

Peruvian intelligence sources told Reuters a U.S. spy plane has made several high-altitude night flights over the site of Peru's hostage siege, gathering information for a possible attack on guerrillas inside.

And anti-terrorism police said crack troops were training at a secret location in Lima around a model of the residence in case of a last-resort attack. But freed hostages have warned against trying to overpower the guerrillas, who are armed with grenades, other explosives, AKM automatic rifles and ample ammunition.
On Friday morning, witnesses said they could see a man cleaning the interior of the building with a broom but reported no other movement at the site.

A former hostage, medical doctor Victor Lucero Rondon, said in a newspaper interview on Friday three of the captives were running serious health risks. But Red Cross members told a news conference their doctors were being allowed to take in medicines and treat hostages.

Red Cross spokesman Ronald Bigler added that members of the organisation had quizzed the rebels about the location of mines and "knew where to put and where not to put their feet" as they came in and out of the residence.
